The Past Perfect vs. The Simple Past
You use both the Simple Past and the Past Perfect tenses to talk about past events. Sometimes you need or want to be precise about the order of events or emphasize which events happened before.

You use the Simple Past to sequence past events or actions.
You can use the Simple Past to put events in chronological order.
You use the Past Perfect tense to refer to an event out of order - to identify which event happened before the last event in the sequence.

Take a look at this example:
I called Joe to thank him for the present he had given me last week.

This sentence contains both the Simple Present and Past Perfect tenses.
Which event happened first? Joe had given me a present.
Which event happened next? I called Joe.
The form of the Past Perfect is:
Last year when I visited, he had just started kindergarten.
His teacher had asked his class to find out about their family that week.
I had just sat down for a nice cup of tea on Saturday before breakfast when he made himself comfortable on the sofa next to me.
He had sat there contemplating for a bit while he sipped some hot chocolate.
He had made a mental list of things to ask about before he commenced.
When we dispensed with my life, we had gone on to looking at the changes in the earth.

Instructions: Complete the following steps. Fill in the Self-Assessment.

images.text:
My grandson has always been precocious and inquisitive. Last year when I visited, he had just started kindergarten. He was learning about the past and asked question after question. His teacher had asked his class to find out about their family that week. He grilled me that weekend in a polite, but persistent way.
I had just sat down for a nice cup of tea on Saturday before breakfast when he made himself comfortable on the sofa next to me. He had sat there contemplating for a bit while he sipped some hot chocolate. His first question caught me off guard and after that he went on relentlessly. I wanted to laugh but didn't dare.

“How old are you Gamma?” he dove in.
“Quite old, but not really old yet”, I parried.
“Were there cars when you were little?” he went on.
“Yes, dear, there were. Our family always had a car.”
“What about phones and internet?” he asked pointedly.
“There were phones,” I countered, “but only at home. We didn't have cell phones and there were no computers except at universities. They weren't like the ones we have today.”

He had obviously wondered about these things. He had made a mental list of things to ask about before he commenced. He wanted answers and evidently felt that I, the oldest of the clan, could best supply them. At that point I got up and found the laptop. I opened it and looked for a timeline.
There we sat through several cups of tea, toast and cereal. When we dispensed with my life, we had gone on to looking at the changes in the earth. Then we tackled modern gadgets and appliances - things he was familiar with.
He was shocked and amazed. He found it difficult to understand how anyone could live without a fridge, a stove or an air conditioner. I often wonder that myself.
